events.title: Telegram
events.text:
🇫🇷⚡️ — French aerospace company Safran has released a video offering a glimpse of some of the technologies being developed for the Dassault Rafale F5, the next major upgrade of the French multirole fighter.
The F5 standard will bring upgrades to the aircraft's propulsion, radar, electronic warfare and combat systems.
One of the main developments is Safran's M88 T-REX engine, designed to increase maximum afterburning thrust by approximately 20%, from 7.5 to 9 tonnes. The upgrades include a redesigned low-pressure compressor, a high-pressure turbine using new materials and advanced cooling systems, and an aerodynamically optimized exhaust nozzle. Despite these changes, the engine will retain the M88's modular architecture, dimensions and maintenance advantages.
The Rafale F5 will also receive Thales' RBE2-XG (eXtended Generation) AESA fire-control radar. Designed to fit within the existing RBE2 nose envelope, the new radar will replace the current RBE2-AA's gallium arsenide (GaAs) technology with gallium nitride (GaN). This will allow it to operate at higher power levels, extending its detection range and improving its ability to detect and identify targets with very low radar cross-sections. The radar will also have greater computing power to support artificial intelligence applications, along with improved resistance to electronic warfare and cyber threats.
The aircraft's electronic warfare and self-protection suite will be upgraded to the SPECTRA F5 standard, developed by Thales and MBDA. The new version will use an all-digital architecture, with improved threat detection and jamming capabilities to deal with increasingly sophisticated air-defence systems.
Another addition will be Thales' Inter-Vehicle Data Link (IVDL), a high-bandwidth communications system designed to provide secure, low-observable and jamming-resistant links between aircraft. It will allow Rafale F5 fighters to share information and coordinate their actions in heavily contested environments.
The Rafale F5 will also be designed to operate alongside a new stealth combat drone, being developed by Dassault Aviation, Thales and Safran. Building on experience gained from the nEUROn demonstrator, the unmanned aircraft will support the Rafale in air-to-air and air-to-ground missions. Its intended roles include penetrating hostile airspace and suppressing enemy air defences. The drone will incorporate low-observable features, advanced sensors, artificial intelligence and resilient communications.
The F5 will also be compatible with France's future ASN4G hypersonic nuclear air-launched missile, which is set to replace the ASMPA-R in the country's airborne nuclear deterrent.
The French Directorate General of Armaments (DGA) is targeting qualification of the Rafale F5 around 2033, ahead of its entry into service with the French Air and Space Force and the French Navy.

🇮🇷 IRGC Navy vows to avenge sailors lost aboard the Dena, other warships
 
The “unjust and arrogant enemy” will be made to understand that “taking revenge for the martyrs of the sea is a pledge we made with our brothers in the Army Navy, sealed in blood,” the IRGC said in a statement Saturday commemorating Navy Day.
🗣 “Salute to the martyrs of the warships Joshan, Sahand, Sabalan and Dena; and salute to our comrades in the Navy of the Islamic Republic of Iran Army,” the IRGC added.
A US submarine destroyed the IRIS Dena frigate on March 4 as it was returning from wargames hosted by India. The ship was unarmed and never got a chance to fight; 104 of its 136 crewmembers were killed. Iranian officials and media dubbed the sinking a “cowardly act.”
The Joshan, Sahand and Sabalan were destroyed in 1988 after the US frigate USS Samuel B. Roberts hit an Iranian naval mine during [the Iran-Iraq Tanker Wars](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/66497).
During February’s surprise attack, the US and Israel also destroyed several other warships, including the IRIS Bayandor and Naghdi corvettes, and the IRIS Jamaran frigate, while they were moored in port.
Iran’s Navy suffered the gravest damage among all military branches and the IRGC in the 2026 war, owing to its collection of large, hard-to-shield vessels clearly visible on satellite and within range of US strike systems. The IRGC’s fleet enjoyed much greater survivability owing to its small, fast-boat fleet, minisubs and protection inside [fortified coastal bases](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/68832), while its ‘missile’ cities have proven virtually unassailable.
While President Trump has boasted repeatedly about “wiping out” and “obliterating” Iran’s Navy, US warships have paradoxically stayed hundreds of nautical miles offshore to avoid being targeted, leaving Iran in near-total strategic control of the Gulf and Hormuz despite its maritime losses.

events.text:
👁 British contractors silently subjugate Lebanon’s security as UNIFIL departure looms
As UNIFIL’s mandate approaches[ its end on December 31](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/78426), British firms embedded inside Lebanon’s military and police institutions are expanding their reach into the south, raising questions about who will control the security vacuum left behind, The Cradle reports.
🔶 ARK Group was awarded a $6.6 million contract by the UK Foreign Office to support Lebanese Armed Forces border security. The work is primarily along the Lebanese-Syrian border, yet the contract explicitly provides «flexibility to support authorised activity in southern Lebanon»
🔶 Siren Associates holds a $22.5 million contract running until March 2028 to strengthen the Internal Security Forces and improve coordination with the army, «including in the South Litani Sector»
Both private security contractors cover training, logistics, vehicle maintenance, and strategic and operational support for Lebanese security forces and have a long history of cooperation with local authorities. At the same time, both carry a trail of British influence in the region:
➡️ During the Syrian war, ARK Group ran British-funded programs supporting media activists and opposition factions, training over 150 journalists and working with 14 radio stations. A 2016 Guardian investigation found British contractors were effectively operating a press office for opposition fighters while concealing the government’s role
➡️ Leaked documents show Siren has worked with the local security forces since 2008, building close ties with senior commanders and identifying officials capable of driving British-backed reforms
The British government has not hidden its objective. During a House of Commons debate in July 2026, minister Hamish Falconer said Lebanese security forces, not Hezbollah, must control the entire country, and described UK assistance as serving British interests.
Unlike UNIFIL, these contractors operate through commercial agreements disclosed only in outline. The Lebanese public is told little about their personnel, access, reporting lines, or what happens when their work conflicts with national interests. Private firms, meanwhile, reshape the security environment without passing through the political scrutiny a formal foreign deployment would attract.

🇵🇱🪖📉 Poland Sinks Deeper Into Debt to Fund Military Buildup
Poland is borrowing to equip its own army and has told NATO it will put no more money, for now, into buying US weapons for Ukraine. Prime Minister Donald Tusk gave NATO chief Mark Rutte two reasons for that decision this month. Poland already has a large budget deficit, and its own defense orders take priority.
One tank order shows how far those commitments run. Poland took delivery of the last of its first 180 South Korean K2 tanks in November 2025. By then it had already signed a second contract with Hyundai Rotem, worth about $6.5B, for another 180 tanks, support equipment and the technology to build some of them in Poland. Deliveries under that order are due to run through 2030.
To finance the deal, Poland’s state development bank signed loan agreements with Santander and South Korea’s export-import bank. That lets Poland place orders years ahead of delivery. It also means the country can take on debt before the equipment reaches its army.
The European Commission expects Poland’s economy to grow 3.5% this year, yet it forecasts a deficit of 7.1% of GDP in both 2026 and 2027. Social benefits and interest payments are already weighing on the budget. By 2028, the Commission expects public debt to reach 73.5% of GDP, up from 59.6% in 2025.
Even the revenue increases in next year’s draft budget face a political hurdle. President Karol Nawrocki can veto legislation, and parliamentary elections are due in 2027. Moody’s cut Poland’s credit rating in September. On November 6, S&P cut its rating on Poland’s local-currency debt and kept its foreign-currency rating at A−, with a negative outlook.
Tusk’s government still plans to spend 4.51% of GDP on defense in 2027. The spending it has put on hold is Poland’s next contribution to a NATO program that pools allied money for US arms and ammunition for Kiev, including missiles for Patriot air defenses. Tusk says other Polish support for Ukraine will continue.
That leaves NATO’s other donors with a concrete choice. If they want to keep those US weapons packages funded at the same level, they will have to cover the share Poland is now unwilling to pay.
